{{More footnotes|date=April 2021}}

In [[stability theory]], the '''Briggs–Bers criterion''' is a criterion for determining whether the [[trivial solution]] to a linear [[partial differential equation]] with [[constant coefficients]] is stable, [[convective instability (stability theory)|convectively unstable]] or [[absolute instability|absolutely unstable]]. This is often useful in [[applied mathematics]], especially in [[fluid dynamics]], because [[linear PDEs]] often govern [[small perturbations]] to a system, and we are interested in whether such perturbations grow or decay. The Briggs–Bers criterion is named after [[R. J. Briggs]] and [[A. Bers]].<ref name="ejb-thesis">{{cite journal|last=Brambley|first=Edward James|title=The acoustics of curved and lined cylindrical ducts with mean flow|date=2007|journal=PhD Thesis}}</ref>

Suppose that the PDE is of the form <math>Ly=0</math>, where <math>y = y(x,t)</math> is a [[function of space and time]](<math>x</math> and <math>t</math>). The [[partial differential operator]] <math>L=L(\partial_x,\partial_t)</math> has constant coefficients, which do not depend on <math>x</math> and <math>t</math>. Then a suitable [[ansatz]] for <math>y</math> is the [[normal mode]] solution 
:<math>y=\hat{y} \exp(ikx-i\omega t).</math>
Making this ansatz is equivalent to considering the problem in [[Fourier space]] – the solution may be decomposed into its [[Fourier components]] in space and time. Making this ansatz, the equation becomes
:<math>L(ik,-i\omega)\hat{y} \exp(ikx-i\omega t) = 0;</math>
or, more simply,
:<math>L(ik,-i\omega) = 0.</math>
This is a [[dispersion relation]] between <math>k</math> and <math>\omega</math>, and tells us how each Fourier component evolves in time. In general, the dispersion relation may be very complicated, and there may be multiple <math>\omega</math> which satisfy the relation for a given value of <math>k</math>, or vice versa. The solutions to the dispersion relation may be complex-valued.<ref name="ejb-thesis"/>

Now, an initial condition <math>y(x,0)</math> can be written as a superposition of Fourier modes of the form <math>\exp(ikx)</math>. In practice, the initial condition will have components of all frequencies. Each of these components evolves according to the dispersion relation, and therefore the solution at a later time <math>y(x,t)</math> may be obtained by Fourier inversion. In the simple case where <math>L</math> is first-order in time, the dispersion relation determines a unique value of <math>\omega(k)</math> for each given value of <math>k</math>, and so
:<math>y(x,t) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int \hat{y}(k) \exp(ikx-i\omega(k)t) \, dk</math>
where
:<math>\hat{y}(k) = \int y(x,0) \exp(-ikx) \, dx</math>
is the Fourier transform of the initial condition. In the more general case, the Fourier inversion must be performed by [[contour integration]] in the complex <math>k</math> and <math>\omega</math> planes.<ref name="ejb-thesis"/>

While it may not be possible to evaluate the integrals explicitly, asymptotic properties of <math>y(x,t)</math> as <math>t\rightarrow\infty</math> may be obtained from the integral expression, using methods such as the [[method of stationary phase]] or the [[method of steepest descent]]. In particular, we can determine whether <math>y(x,t)</math> decays or grows exponentially in time, by considering the largest value that <math>\Im\omega</math> may take. If the dispersion relation is such that <math>\Im\omega<0</math> always, then any solution will decay as <math>t\rightarrow\infty</math>, and the trivial solution <math>y=0</math> is stable. If there is some mode with <math>\Im\omega>0</math>, then that mode grows exponentially in time. By considering modes with zero [[group velocity]] and determining whether they grow or decay, we can determine whether an initial condition which is localised around <math>x=0</math> moves away from <math>x=0</math> as it grows, with <math>y(0,t)\rightarrow 0</math> (convective instability); or whether <math>y(0,t)\rightarrow\infty</math> (absolute instability).

==Transient growth==
Suppose the PDE is of the form
:<math>y_t = A y</math>
where <math>A</math> is a linear differential operator in <math>x</math>. In general, <math>A</math> is not a [[normal operator]]. While the large-time behaviour of <math>y</math> is still determined by the [[eigenvalues]] of <math>A</math>, the behaviour which takes place before this large-time behaviour may be dramatically different.<ref name="chomaz-2005">{{cite journal|last1=Chomaz|first1=Jean-Marc|title=Global instabilities in spatially developing flows: Non-normality and nonlinearity.|journal=Annu. Rev. Fluid Mech.|date=2005|volume=37 |issue=1 |page=357 |doi=10.1146/annurev.fluid.37.061903.175810 |bibcode=2005AnRFM..37..357C |url=https://hal-polytechnique.archives-ouvertes.fr/hal-01024960/file/JMCG.pdf }}</ref>

In particular, while the eigenvalues of <math>A</math> may all have negative real part, which would predict that <math>y</math> decays exponentially at large times and that the trivial state <math>y=0</math> is stable, it is possible for <math>y</math> to grow transiently and become large before decaying.<ref name="chomaz-2005"/> In practice, the linear equations that we work with are [[linearisation]]s of more complicated governing equations such as the [[Navier–Stokes equations]] about some base state, with the linearisations carried out under the assumption that the perturbation quantity <math>y</math> is small. Transient growth may violate this assumption. When nonlinear effects are considered, then a system may be unstable even if the linearised system is stable.

==Generalisation==
When the coefficients of <math>L</math> vary with <math>x</math>, then this criterion is no longer applicable. However, if the variation is very slow, then the [[WKBJ approximation]] may be used to derive a leading-order approximation to the solution. This gives rise to the theory of [[global mode]]s, which was first developed by [[Philip Drazin]] in 1974.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Drazin|first1=Philip | authorlink1=Philip Drazin | date=1974|title=On a model of instability of a slowly-varying flow|journal=Q J Mechanics Appl Math|volume=27 |pages=69–86 |doi=10.1093/qjmam/27.1.69 }}</ref>
